en: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dàhuì Pǔjué, Resident of Néngrén Chan Monastery at Jìngshān, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Dharma Heir and Abbot of Néngrén Chan Monastery at Jìngshān.

I, the subject Yunwen, Chan Master Huiri, respectfully submit this report: On the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Shaoxing era, the Master opened the hall at Mingqing Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture.
Holding up the commentary, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Chancellor, Lord Liushi,
has entered the samādhi of skillfully knowing all arts."
Having emitted great radiance from the tip of the writing brush and finished expounding the forty-two gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* without moving the tongue,
do you still believe this?
If your faith is insufficient,
please request the *biaobai* (the formal announcement) once more,
so that it may be brought forth anew.
He caused those who had not heard to hear and those who had not believed to believe.
Expounding the commentary and pointing toward the Dharma seat, he summoned the great assembly, saying: "Do you see?"
Seated, he cuts off the path of the ancient Buddhas;
a thousand demons and a hundred monsters hide away in terror.
Even were it Mount Sumeru or King Dīpa, they would be no match.
One must quickly perform three prostrations and let out one shout.
Then, ascending the seat, he holds up the incense and says:
"This single offering of incense."
I reverently offer incense to pray for the ten-thousand-year longevity of the Most Honored One at the Northern Palace, and further to wish for the myriad blessings of Mount Nan.
Next, he picks up the incense and says:

This single portion of incense is offered on behalf of the Grand Chancellor, the Imperial Resident, as well as the civil and military officials, that they may forever abide in their positions of honor and rank.
Again, he takes up the incense and says:
This single offering of incense:
if you gaze upon it, your eyes will wither;
if you smell it, your skull will split open.
When encountered by the noble, its value is esteemed in this Sahā world;
when encountered by the lowly, it is not worth a single coin.
Today, before the assembly of devas and humans:
Incense is burned within the incense burner.
This is offered on behalf of the late Great Master Chan Master Yuanwu of Zhaojue Chan Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture,
in order to repay the kindness of his Dharma-milk.
Thereupon, he ascended the seat and struck the gavel, saying:
"O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast,
you should contemplate the primary truth."
The Master said:
"This is the established precedent of all quarters and the constant ritual of both past and present.

Even if the thousand Buddhas and World-Honored Ones were to appear in succession and ascend this seat, they would still lack this single ladle of foul water; there is no one who can avoid it. Is there anyone here who can come forward and provide proof?"
At that time, a monk came forward to prostrate.
The Master said,
"Adding frost to snow."
Next, a monk stepped forward and asked:
"The assembly of humans and devas has gathered and the field for selecting Buddhas has opened;
how should the Patriarchal command be proclaimed when the occasion arises?"
The Master said,
"A dull bird flies against the wind.
The student asked, "What then?"
Throughout the entire world there is no place to seek;
clearly manifest, a single point is perfect within the seat.
The Master said:
"Among humans, there is none who does not face east.
The student said,
"One might say that the Bodhi tree has borne its fruit through the three springs."
"In a single night the flowers bloom, and the world is fragrant.
The Master said,
"It strikes right where it hits."
The student said:
"A profusion of fragrant incense issues from the burner;
a refreshing breeze arises upon the seat."
The Master said,
"Idle words. The student stepped forward and asked:
Alas, how regrettable! A thousand branches of the Shaoshi flowers are now in full bloom;
a single stream of the Cao Yuan waters is even clearer.
The Master raised his whisk and said:
This is the first branch of the pivot.
[The student] advances and says:
"One who knows the sound does not need to raise it repeatedly."
"One who has attained must know the shock within the darkness.
The Master said, "A sharp and discerning monk asked: [The monk] asked.
To engage in a single question and answer is to辜负 (betray) one’s own spiritual nature;
to cite ancient and modern precedents is to bury the ancestors.
Setting aside these two paths, how can one be thus?
The Master said,
"Look at the divided body in two places.
The student stepped forward and asked:
In the land of Tang, two or three people fold their robes in reverence;
even among the four or seven patriarchs of the Western Heaven, they too raise their eyebrows.
The Master said:
"Heaven covers all without partiality; Earth bears all without partiality.
The student said, "A dialogue such as this already involves the traces of effort and achievement."
"Recite one phrase for the consecration; please, Master, speak quickly.
The Master said:
"Constantly take the sun and moon as your celestial eye."
He pointed out that Mount Sumeru serves as the mountain of longevity.
The Master continued:
"The altars of state and the mountains and rivers increase their vital energy."
"Heaven and earth, grasses and trees— all receive this grace.
The Master said,
"To speak a verse once more."
The student asked,
"Do you permit me to reveal another message?
The Master said:
"Not permitted.
The student replied,
"I request the Master to speak instead."
The Master said,
"Since you are not permitted to speak further, what else could there be? The student stepped forward and asked:
"I pray that you grant me the hands of Zhu Yun to break the wooden barriers;
may you come as the man of Fu Yue to bring down the rains.
The Master said:
"It was only lacking this one phrase.
Several monks then vied with one another to step forward,
whereupon the Master called them back and said:
Suppose the grasses and trees of the great earth were all ground into dust;
if each grain of dust possessed a mouth,
and each mouth were endowed with the mark of a broad and long tongue free from obstruction.
From each and every mark of the tongue emerge immeasurable varieties of sounds;
from each and every sound issue immeasurable varieties of expressions;
and within each and every expression lie immeasurable varieties of wondrous meanings.
Suppose as many monks as there are motes of dust each possessed such mouths, such tongues, such voices, such speech, and such wondrous meanings,
and simultaneously posed hundreds of thousands of difficult questions.
If each question were answered individually, it would not suffice;
yet the Elder of Jing Mountain coughed once and answered them all at once.
Seizing that moment, he performed immeasurable, boundless, and vast Buddha-work within that single instant.
Each and every Buddha-activity pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
that is to say, a single hair-pore manifests spiritual transformations,
and all Buddhas together preach the sutras.
Even throughout immeasurable kalpas, one cannot reach its limit; yet,
if one simply proceeds in this manner,
one will succeed in the bustling gateway of the patriarchal hall.
If one observes with the correct eye,
this is precisely the state where karmic consciousness is vast and茫然 (vastly wandering), having no fundamental basis to rely upon;
not even a single point is of any use within the Gate of the Patriarchs.
How much more so when they employ hooks and thorns, exposing their verbal acumen;
not only do they bury the ancestral vehicle of the patriarchs,
but they also laugh until the nostrils of the monks are split asunder.
Thus it is said: "To harbor even a hair’s breadth of attachment is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms;
for a fleeting thought to arise is to be bound by shackles for ten thousand kalpas.
Whether called 'sage' or 'ordinary person,' these are all but empty sounds."
Exquisite features and inferior forms are all illusory appearances.
If you seek them, will you not incur entanglement?
And when you grow weary of them, they become a great affliction.
Observe how the former masters made such announcements;
they were like the weapons of a state, employed only when there was no other recourse.
Even within the matter of one's own fundamental nature, there is not even a trace of this.
Today, this mountain monk’s raising of such a theme is much like speaking of a dream while dreaming;
it is like gouging a sore on healthy flesh. When scrutinized, he deserves to be struck.
As for this staff, is there anyone here now who can bring down the lethal blow?
If there is one capable of repaying the unrequited debt of gratitude,
let us together assist in the transformation of non-action.
"Just as one proceeds without error,
this causes one to go.
[The Master] suddenly picked up his staff and said:
Horizontally grasping the Mohe sword, he maintains the perfect command;
in this world of Great Peace, he slays the foolish and the stubborn.
*He strikes once.*
[The Master] let out a shout; the words of thanks are not recorded.
Again, he raised the case: One day, Attendant Wang visited Linji.
They went together into the Sangha Hall.
The Attendant asked,
"Do the monks in this hall look at the scriptures from a distance?
Linji replied:
He did not look at the sutras.
The Attendant asked,
"Do you practice Chan?"
Linji said, "I do not study Chan.
Changshi asked, "Why?"
"If you neither read the sutras nor study Chan,
what exactly are you doing? Linji said.
"Generally, I teach them to become Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Changshi said, "Though gold dust is precious, when it falls into the eye it becomes a cataract; what then?"
Linji said, "I took you for a mere worldly man.
The Master replied:
The old man Linji wields a blade of the Vajra King;
his spirit pierces the universe,
and he roams freely across the world.
Inadvertently pressed by this official with a light nudge, it immediately dissolves like melting ice and crumbling walls.
Now tell me: how was this?
"What excellence does this official possess?
Listen to this verse:
'A rare occurrence, both mundane and supramundane.'"
To manifest [the truth], one must rely on a person of transcendent capacity;
using only the hands that once mended robes and stirred soup,
they turn the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
The assembly has stood for a long time;
I humbly entreat you all to take care of yourselves.
The presiding officer strikes the mallet once more and says:
Contemplate deeply the Dharma of the Dharma King;
such is the Dharma of the Dharma King.
Entering the hall for the formal lecture.
When this mountain monk had not yet departed from Quanzhou, I had already met you all;
at Lin’an Prefecture as well, I had already met you all.
When they arrived at the mountain, they struck the Dharma drum and sat and stood with solemn dignity, gazing intently at one another.
Why, then, did they not recognize each other?
It was simply because it was too clear.
This only causes what you have attained to be delayed.
Tonight there will be a small *sengcan* (private instruction).
The Great Way is right before your mouths.
For the time being, it is difficult to behold directly.
Yet, if you wish to recognize the true essence of the Great Way,
it is not separate from sound, form, and speech.
Raising the whisk, he said:
"This is form. Striking the meditation seat, he said:
This is sound. This mountain monk is now speaking with his mouth flapping;
that is speech. Which, then, is the true essence of the Great Way?
He gave a shout and said:
"This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing;
there is no further sound or form to present to you."
If one realizes within this that there is nothing at all,
then essence and function are neither obstructed nor distinguished.
Should they be distinguished:
When rain falls, the ground becomes wet;
when the sky clears, the sun comes out.
A short month has twenty-nine days.
The thirtieth day of the month has ended.
If [the land] is not divided,
Vajra and the local deity will rub his back with their hands until a bone protrudes.
It is further said:
"The ancients taught that the final phrase is where one finally reaches the secure barrier."
Severing the vital ford so that neither ordinary nor sage may pass— what is this final phrase?
After a long silence, he said:
"Stop talking about dreams.
He struck the meditation seat and descended from it. Then he ascended the hall for the formal discourse.
In the past, the ancient patriarch Yangqi plowed and pulled the harrow.
Those who display supernatural powers are but descendants dragging through water and mud;
a tea cauldron is not the same as an iron smoothing-iron.
Ascending the hall,
[the Master] raised an example: A monk asked Lishan,
"All forms return to emptiness."
"Where do you return when empty-handed?
The mountain said,
"The tongue does not leave the mouth."
The monk asked,
"Why is it so? Sanshan replied:
Because inner and outer are as one.
The Master said:
"The matter lies in the meeting of the box and its lid."
In principle, it should be like the tip of an arrow meeting its target;
one must return to Mount Li before it can be attained.
If it were Mount Jing, it would not be so.
Someone asked: "Where do all forms return when they dissolve into emptiness, and where does that emptiness return?
"The peony flower blooms upon the face of a Bodhisattva;
the palm leaves scatter upon the head of a yakṣa."
Why is this so? Simply prepare a heart of resolve,
and you will certainly not be deceived.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: Nanquan said,
"In Jiangxi, Mazu says 'this very mind is Buddha.'"
Master Wang does not speak in this way.
"It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing"—
this is how he speaks.
"Is there anything further?
Zhaozhou bowed and departed.
At that time, a monk followed him and asked Zhaozhou:
After the Elder had prostrated and departed,
[Zhaozhou] asked, "What was his intention? Zhaozhou said:
"You should go back and ask your Preceptor.
The monk went up and asked,
"What was the meaning of that just now, Elder Shen?"
Quan said, "He indeed grasped the old monk's meaning.
The Master said:
Although these two old fellows are skilled at moving their fingers within their boots,
they fail to realize that the onlooker sees the ugliness.
This was the great memorial service for Master Yuanwu.
Holding up the incense, he points to the true nature and says:
"This Sichuan fellow has always been fond of making a commotion."
He enters the fray wherever there is clamor;
he loathes stillness and delights in motion.
On this very day last year, he finally returned home.
"Today, the path from last year is no different," he said,
looking back at the assembly and asking,
"What is this path that is not different?"
Do you understand?
Each time one drinks water, there is a moment of obscuration;
each piece of sandalwood incense and each bowl of tea is likewise so.
He then burned incense,
ascended the hall,
took up his staff, struck it once, and let out a shout, saying:
Fortunately, you are already pitiable enough.
Why do you needlessly strike and shout in such disorder?
What is the point?
He threw it down and said:
"When you are in a cold place, hold a fire.
Then he ascended the hall.
This morning is the fifteenth day of the eighth month;
who does not behold the hare in the sky?
Were it not for the little Śākyamuni of the Eastern Land, [this would not be so].
Letting go of this tiger of Changsha.
Entering the hall,
the Patriarch said:
When the single mind does not arise,
the myriad dharmas are without fault. When there is no fault, there are no dharmas.
Neither arising nor mind,
they can follow the objects until they cease;
as the objects subside, the faculties sink along with them.
The object is established by the subject; the subject is established by the capacity of the object.
Yet the great and small patriarchs have instead adopted the perspective of a scholastic master.
At Jingshan, it is not so:
the eye does not see itself;
a blade does not cut itself.
Eating food relieves hunger;
drinking water quenches thirst.
Linji and Deshan have, for no reason, needlessly caused confusion.
To expend one's spirit in bestowing blows and shouts—
set aside the blows and cast away the shouts!
You fellow from Meng Village!
"How does one bring it to rest?
He ascended the hall and said:
"Subhūti was sitting in meditative seclusion within a mountain cave."
The devas rained down flowers and praised the Venerable One, saying:
"Who is this person raining flowers from the air and offering praise?
He replied: "I am Brahmā."
The Venerable One asked,
"How do you offer praise?
The deva replied:
"I revere the Venerable One’s excellent exposition of Prajñāpāramitā.
The Venerable One replied,
"I have never uttered a single word regarding Prajñāpāramitā."
"How can you say it was well-spoken?
The Master let out a shout and said,
"If you had been able to let fall this one shout at that moment..."
"Not only has he stopped the mouth of Brahmā,
but he shall also escape being scrutinized by Jingshan two thousand years hence. Tian said:
"Venerable One, there is nothing to be said;
I, therefore, have nothing to hear.
This absence of what is said and what is heard is the true teaching of Prajñāpāramitā."
The Master again gave a shout and said:
"If he had been able to let out this very shout at that moment,
it would have not only stopped Subhūti’s mouth."
Thus, even two thousand years later, one may avoid being scrutinized by Jingshan.
But tell me:
does Jingshan himself have any place where he might be scrutinized by others?
He said to himself,
"What place is there for me to be scrutinized by others?
It is not right to be so talkative."
Ascending the hall, he said:
"The mud ox at the bottom of the water chews raw iron;
Gavāmpati bites his own tongue."
The Sea God, enraged, brandishes his coral whip;
Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, suffers unbearable pain.
[With this,] he strikes the meditation seat and descends from it.
Ascending the hall, he said:
"Piercing through the azure void, a thousand-foot pine;
cutting off the red dust, a stream of water."
Failing to recognize one's original true face,
one thinks that someone else has composed a poem for Deqiao.
This is what Lin'an County says.
He opened the hall at Haihui Temple.
The Master held up the ceremonial document and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Before the patterns of the text have even appeared, the message has already been revealed."
Once the patterns and brilliance have been manifested, they are difficult to conceal;
since they cannot be concealed, it is necessary to trouble you with this formal declaration.
Having read the commentary aloud once,
the Master looked over the assembly and said,
"The Magistrate-Scholar has already expounded the primary truth for all of you."
Is there anyone who has opened their eyes and attained awakening?
If so, please come forward;
otherwise, disperse at once.
If this were not yet so, I, Qingshan,
would instead speak empty falsehoods from atop my curved wooden seat. Thereupon,
he ascended the seat and offered incense.
Having finished the ritual for honoring the Sage, he again holds up the incense and says:
"This one portion of incense is unknown to all Buddhas."
It is unfathomable even to spirits and deities;
it is not something produced by Heaven and Earth,
nor is it something obtained through spontaneous occurrence.
Yesterday, I already brought this up within the city.
Today, as the assembly of humans and devas has gathered and the fourfold community has all arrived,
there may be among them those who have not yet caught its scent.
Unable to avoid explaining it once more,
he then lit the incense and took his seat.
A monk asked:
The wind of Yao’s virtue has fanned forever;
the Bodhisattva manifests in the body of a high-ranking official.
The sun of the Buddha is lofty and bright.
The Old Man Lu sings the song of Shaolin.
To celebrate the Emperor’s birthday and open the hall, he wishes to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
The Master said:
It shook heaven and moved earth.
[The student] stepped forward and said,
"Relying upon a single drop of Master’s Caoxi water."
"Bringing rain to the four seas to repay my Sovereign.
The Master said:
"A single wild goose has just returned; autumn fills the four seas."
The attendant said:
"The Golden Wheel governs the three thousand worlds;
the Jade Calendar extends a hundred thousand springs."
The Master said,
"Who would not wish for this?
He asked.
Third, regarding the Holy Path:
whenever I encounter people, I manifest it;
yet once manifested, it does not belong to them.
"What is the meaning?
The Master said,
"To kill a person, one does not need a sword."
Jin said: "Xinghua said, 'Whenever I meet a person, I do not come out;
when I do come out, I do so for the sake of others.'"
"Furthermore, how is it?
The Master said,
"Why does one who brings the living back to life need a sword?"
Jin asked, "At the very moment when it is about to emerge, but has not yet emerged, what is it like?
The Master said:
The hairless chain rattles at both ends.
He replied, "I am specifically going to propagate it."
The Master said:
"Today Jingshan has suffered a loss," and then he added:
"The ultimate point of the Buddha-dharma does not reside in the place of question and answer."
Even if one were to question like the clouds arising from Samantabhadra’s Wisdom and answer like the pouring of water from Samantabhadra’s Vase,
if one does not recognize its essential subtlety, [it is all in vain].
This results in nothing more than mere theatrical talk;
what benefit does it provide for the Way?
To speak according to reality:
All are merely deluded and frantic, wandering outside. Therefore,
for the sake of the one great cause and condition, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One appeared in the world,
employing various subtle, secret, and skillful means to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
He revealed, awakened to, and entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
rising from the Bodhi tree, he proceeded to the Deer Park and first turned the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths for Kauṇḍinya and the others.
Over forty-nine years, in more than three hundred and sixty assemblies,
he sequentially expounded the teachings according to what was appropriate for the faculties and capacities of sentient beings,
causing each of them to hear the Dharma, attain realization, and transcend birth and death.
At the very end, when he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
before an assembly of a million beings among gods and humans,
he held up a flower and showed it universally.
Only the ascetic Suvarṇavarṇa broke into a smile and said,
"I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa."
I entrust this to you. From that time forth,
through the four groups of seven in the Western Heaven and the two groups of three in the Eastern Land,
the elder monks throughout the world have each transmitted mind-to-mind in an uninterrupted succession.
Had they not recognized its essential subtlety,
but instead remained solely immersed in intellectual views and indulged in the proliferation of words,
how could the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye have been transmitted to this day?
To reach this point, one must be an extraordinary person who seeks nothing from the sages and values nothing of their own spiritual self; only such a one can shoulder this great matter.
Now, who is that extraordinary person?
It is not seen that in the past, Mazu Daishi of Jiangxi dispatched Xitang Zhizang to deliver a letter to National Master Guoyi of Mount Jing.
Upon opening the needle-case, he saw a single circular mark.
He then requested a brush and, facing Zhizang,
placed a single dot within the circle.
Zhizang was at a loss for words.
Is this not a message that transcends the ordinary? If one were to deliberate upon it as something beyond the ordinary, [one would miss the point].
Furthermore, it is not so.
How, then, do you all distinguish this?
How do you make use of it within the midst of time?
In the memorial recently submitted by the Magistrate-Scholar, it was stated:
"Master Ma’s circular diagrams (yuanxiang) have transmitted pure regulations from afar across a thousand li;
Old Qin’s sharp wit has pierced through the delusions of the multitude of this age."
Once the multitude of delusions has been shattered,
then for every person, the great matter beneath their own feet will be clearly illuminated.
Once the great matter is clear, [the path is open].

Thus, throughout the twelve periods of the day, whether turning, walking, bowing, looking up, snapping fingers, or clearing one's throat, every action is none other than the wondrous function of the Buddha.
Since these are the wondrous functions of the Buddha,
they are not obtained from others.
It is not obtained from others,
nor does it reside within one's own person;
since it does not reside within one's own person, [it is ungraspable].
Then, internally one does not emit outward, and externally one does not admit inward.
Since one does not admit anything inward from without, one ceases all external conditions;
internally, one does not emit.
Then the inner mind will be free from labored breathing.
Once the inner mind is free from labored breathing and external conditions are stilled,
then all-encompassing wisdom and spiritual penetration will be without obstruction.
Since there is no obstruction,
the knowledge of all modes is pure,
non-dual, and indivisible.
Because there is neither distinction nor interruption, at this very moment,
it is not a worldly dharma.
Nor is it a supramundane dharma.
To drag [the two nations] together and force Campā and Silla into a head-to-head struggle—
how could this possibly be outside their proper sphere?
Although it is thus, there is yet more to be considered.
I venture to ask you all: [what is it?]
If so, why did National Teacher Zhong say,
"Master Qin was still deluded by Master Ma"?
Is there anyone present now who can provide a definitive judgment on this?
If they are certain to attain liberation,
then you may concede that all such people are indeed extraordinary practitioners of the Way.
"If this is not yet so, Jing-shan shall proceed to finalize the case based on the facts.
After a long silence, he said:
In Śrāvastī it was said that guests were easy to find, yet only upon reaching the fishing trap did one realize how difficult it is to catch the fish.
[The Master] ascended the hall. A monk asked:
On Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa heard it directly;
before the Shao-shi Peak, Shen Guang attained the marrow.
Who among those here today is a true connoisseur?
The Master said,
"It tears the tongue asunder.
The student asked further:
One might say that the workshop of the Bian family abounds with giant uncut gems,
and the gate of Mengchang’s mansion is filled with eminent guests.
The Master said:
"There is no need to laboriously pick out the rubble," [the Master] said.
The student replied,
"But how can one avoid the anomaly before the blade?"
There is no self within the phrase.
The Master said,
"Who is the one who understands?"
The student said:
"Before the cliffs of Shaoshi, the golden phoenix dances;
atop the peaks of Jingshan, the jade rooster crows."
The Master said,
"A case of double layers. [The student] asked.
When Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted the mind-seal directly,
pointing straight at the human mind so that one may see one's nature and attain Buddhahood.
It is just like Deshan, who would strike a student with his staff the moment they entered the gate.
"Linji, upon entering the gate, would immediately shout; I do not know whether this is the same as that or different.
The Master sighed, "Heh heh.
The student continued:
"If it is so, then it is ever serene right where one is;
though you seek it, you will find it cannot be seen.
The Master said:
"When a fish swims, the water becomes turbid.
Jìn said, "What can one do?
It is like treading upon a scale-weight; it is hard as iron."
The Master said,
"Lead [him] so that he does not cling. The student said,
"At every point where instruction is bestowed..."
"Observe this thoroughly and well.
The Master said,
"I grant you thirty blows."
It is then said:
"Do not engage in contrivance; by all means, do not fabricate.
To fabricate and contrive is to bind oneself with no rope."
Without contrivance or fabrication, Sudhana tapped his fingers and ascended the pavilion;
Bimādevī cast down the trident from her hand;
Puhua entered the marketplace shaking his bell.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited Panshan, who said:
"The moon of mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena.
The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist."
When both light and its object have vanished, what is it?
Dongshan said:
"When light and its object have not yet vanished, what is it?"
The Master said:
"A white heron descends to the field—a thousand points of snow;
a yellow oriole perches on a tree—a single branch of blossoms."
Ascending the hall,
a monk asked:
"When Muzhou and Yangshan met back then, they stuck their spades into the ground and stood with hands folded."
"What do you think?
The Master said,
"Two eyes facing two eyes."
Jin said: "On a stringless lute, those who understand its music are few;
father and son play it together, for the tonal style is sublime."
The Master said:
"Now tell me, is it at the place where the spade is thrust in, or is it at the place where the hands are folded?"
Jin said: "The line on the tip of the pole is manipulated by the Master;
without disturbing the clear waves, his intent is naturally distinct."
The Master said,
"And yet, it goes off like this.
He then continued:
The phrase "having a sentence" and "lacking a sentence" are like a vine leaning against a tree;
even the blue-eyed barbarian does not know where they fall.
Tell me, tell me!

He then composed a verse: "Thirty years ago, I met the old fellow at the mountain gate; today, I see him again on the road. The old fellow’s eyebrows are still there, but his face is gone. This is the very point where the karmic consciousness plays with the eyes of a ghost. Is this not to deceive others while deceiving oneself, and to lead others astray while leading oneself astray? Have you not seen this? When Linji was attending upon Deshan... [as above].
Shan Hu returned and looked back,
saying, "May I ask you about something? Ji replied:
"What is this old fellow prattling in his sleep for?
As Shanshan was about to take up his staff,
Linji overturned the meditation seat.
Shan then desisted. Now tell me:
when these two elders thus engaged in such spirited exchange, was there any room for deliberation?
I know with certainty that the trampling of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure;
it is not those who lack true eyes who can attain such function.
Otherwise, one cannot avoid merely calculating and speculating within the realm of gain and loss.
Furthermore, while Linji and Puhua were at Zhenzhou, they went to a donor’s house for a meal. During the meal, Linji asked:
"A hair swallows the vast ocean; a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru."
"Is this the wondrous function of spiritual powers,
or is it simply the nature of things as they are?
Puhua then kicked over the rice table.
Ji said, "Too coarse, sir. Huihua said:
"What place is this? Whether you speak of the coarse or the subtle,
I have already let it rest."
The next day, they went together again to a donor’s vegetarian feast.
Linji asked once more,
"How does today's offering compare with yesterday's?"
Hua also kicked over the rice table.
Ji said, "It is so, it is so;
however, you are too crude."
Huayan said, "Blind fellow, what 'coarse' or 'subtle' Dharma could there possibly be?
Jie then desisted.
Now tell me: when Linji twice told him to "stop," was there still room for deliberation?
If there were, how would one deliberate?
Chan Master Chongmi has resided in the monastic community for the longest time.
Often, one deliberates, explains, and critiques until one considers oneself to have reached a definitive conclusion;
only later does one realize it was mistaken.
Consequently, I set everything aside at once and applied myself to practice in a state free from conceptual deliberation;
only now have I finally been able to perceive it and gain conviction in it.
Only then do you know that this matter cannot be transmitted, cannot be learned, cannot be calculated, and cannot be deliberated upon.
You have attended me as I came from the south,
following me along the shores of desolation.
After four years had passed,
because I raised the question posed by my late teacher to the monk Jishou Dao-ren— "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing"—
I suddenly picked up a single parched bean from beside the brazier and ate it.
From this point on, even the wondrous offerings of the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyuha) no longer attracted his mind;
he simply could not get by on steamed buns alone for even a single meal.

Having come to bid me farewell and return briefly to Zhejiang, he brought this scroll seeking my instruction. He then presented two verses, saying: [Verse 1] The vast expanse of the sky is originally without form; How could it ever be measured by the foot? If you wish to know its true nature, Look directly at your own face. [Verse 2] The great ocean is fundamentally bottomless; How could it ever be fathomed by the cubit? If you wish to know its true source, Observe the reflection within the water.
This one matter that covers heaven and earth— Without past or present, it is beyond all grasping.
Do not vainly hand it over to those who practice "secrecy Chan"; Let the various quarters measure it at will.
Only when the blind donkey has extinguished the Eye of the True Dharma Will the wind of the Linji school begin to spread widely.

"Pitiful are those who trade in the semblance of the Tathāgata; they do nothing but cover it over and engage in erroneous deliberations. To the Dharma Master Shidao Ming, the Dharma Master Shidao Ming: formerly, Mazu asked Master Liang: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Master Liang replied, "The sun rises in the east. Mazu said, "If you can explain this, I will grant you the title of 'Master'. Master Liang was speechless. Mazu said, "I have already granted you the title of 'Master'; why do you still seek it from me? Master Liang was again speechless. Mazu said, "You have been a Master for thirty years; what a pity! Master Liang subsequently went to see Baizhang. Baizhang asked, "Where have you come from? Master Liang replied, "From Mazu. Baizhang said, "What did he say to you when you asked about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Master Liang recounted the previous exchange. Baizhang laughed and said, "He has already granted you the title of 'Master'; why do you still seek it from me? Master Liang was again speechless. Baizhang said, "You have been a Master for thirty years; what a pity! Master Liang was greatly enlightened by this. Later, he went to see Huangbo. Huangbo asked, "Where have you come from? Master Liang replied, "From Baizhang. Huangbo said, "What did he say to you when you asked about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Master Liang recounted the previous exchange. He then passed away. It is said that he had no successor. This is truly a matter of great regret. This is the story of Master Liang. The Master asked, "I have heard that you lecture extensively on the sutras and śāstras; is this true?
He replied, "I dare not say so.
The Master asked again.
"What do you speak about? he asked.
[The monk] replied, "I speak about the mind.
The Patriarch said:
The mind is like a stage performer; the intellect is like the assistant who coordinates the performance.
Furthermore, they compete with one another to explain and expound upon the sutras.
[The monk] asked, "Since the mind cannot be explained,
could it be that empty space can be explained?
The Patriarch said:
However, Xukong lectured on it, and Hui Liang refused to accept this;
he shook out his sleeves and departed.
The Patriarch then called out, "Master of the Seat!
Liang turned his head and was suddenly enlightened.
He then paid his respects and departed,
proceeding directly into the Western Mountains.
There was no other way to convey news except through silence.
Directly beneath, one cuts off the path of both ordinary people and sages.
Nowadays, people seem to have it and yet do not;
or they recognize it merely through the verbal expressions of their teachers.
In wheat there is flour and rice; this rice is made from grain.
Thus, one seeks understanding by searching for it within the wheat and the rice, desiring that the master recognize: "I have already attained this principle."
Fearing that the master might not recognize them,
such as these types of people acknowledge nothing but the "donkey's front" and the "horse's rear."
If you wish to attain the state where, upon a single word from Mazu, you immediately lose all that you have realized—
as Master Liang did— is it not difficult?
For Master Liang was one forged from solid steel and cast from raw iron.
Thus, one can achieve a thousand certainties with a hundredfold precision,
immediately leaping out of the subtle and mysterious nest of the scriptural vehicles,
and instantly severing the continuity of past and future.
There is not a single dharma that can be realized; this is the principle of what is realized and what is not.
Nowadays, when lecturers hear a master say, "It is actually empty space," they proceed to search hither and thither within that very emptiness.
If one does not doubt, there will be no slander.
Master Daoming was also a lecturer on the sutras;
he knew that the decisive point lies certainly not within words and language.
Words and language are but fingers pointing at the moon.

If you wish to seek out a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to understand that single point which is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of written words, and free from the characteristics of mental conceptualization—this is what you must do.
Therefore, you have come to seek out Wondrous Joy (Abhirati).
Wondrous Joy, moved by your utmost sincerity,
has directly recorded this segment of the public case (gong'an) to show you.
One day, suddenly, upon encountering paper, ink, and written words,
one recognizes the message of the separate transmission outside the teachings;
only then does one know that there is no flour within wheat and that rice is not made from grain.
Once you have understood it in this way,
you will be able, even before a single word has been spoken in a lecture,
to make a dead snake writhe and move with lifelike vigor.
To say that space understands the preaching of the sutras,
or that space does not understand the preaching of the sutras—
this is entirely a matter within one's own house.
Within and without the teachings, one no longer harbors views of what is "already realized" or "not yet realized.
Once these two views have vanished,
the very moment of lecturing is itself the moment of not lecturing.
When there is no speaking, that is precisely the time for speaking;
when silent, one speaks, and when speaking, one is silent.
The great gate of giving is opened wide, without any obstruction.
"He is one who speaks the truth, who speaks reality, who speaks according to things as they are, who does not speak deceptively, and who does not speak falsely— ah,
to speak in such a manner is much like recounting a dream while still dreaming."
To open one's eyes and still wet the bed—
to write such things as this deserves thirty blows of the staff as well.
Although this is so,
it merely uses provisional names to guide sentient beings; yet,
this does not hinder one from lecturing on the sutras while simultaneously comprehending the message of the patriarchs’ separate transmission outside the teachings.
Daoming simply continued his practice in this manner.
As he lectured on the sutras and treatises in this way, the paper was exhausted;
for now, let us cut through this web of complications.
To Zen Practitioner Miaozong: An ancient sage said, "The Way does not depend on cultivation;
it simply must not be defiled."
The mountain monk says:
To speak of mind and nature is defilement;
to speak of the mysterious and the wondrous is defilement.
Practicing dhyāna and cultivating samādhi is defilement;
dwelling on thoughts with mental attachment is defilement.
At this very moment, to thus employ paper and brush is itself defilement.
This is merely a case of defilement.
Apart from this, ultimately, what is it?
At the point where one truly gains power,
the adamantine jewel-sword cuts through it at once;
do not concern yourself with right or wrong in the human world.
In general, practice Chan simply in this manner.

Submitted by the Imperial Subject Yunwen, Abbot of Nengren Chan Monastery at Mount Jingshan in the Song Dynasty and Dharma Heir of Chan Master Huirì, in response to Minister Zeng Tianyou.
Question: A letter was sent some time ago when [I] was in Changsha.
I have received a letter from Master Yuanwu,
in which he states that what you have gained from following him in your later years is truly extraordinary and magnificent.
I have reflected upon this again and again.
It has now been eight years;
I have always regretted not having had the opportunity to personally hear even a fragment of your teachings,
and my admiration remains most earnest.
From his youth, Kai resolved his mind on awakening;
he visited and paid homage to spiritual mentors to inquire about this matter.
After reaching the age of twenty, he...
I was immediately bound by the demands of marriage and official service;
my practice lacked purity,
and thus I have followed this course until now, grown old.
I have never heard of such a thing and have always felt ashamed and sighed in regret.
Nevertheless, my resolve and aspiration truly do not lie in the pursuit of shallow knowledge and views.
One might think that if one does not awaken, that is the end of it;
yet once awakened, one must reach the very place where the ancients realized it for themselves before it can be called the ground of great rest.
Although this mind has never for a single moment faltered or retreated, [it remains necessary to reach that ultimate realization].
The practice of self-awakening has not yet reached a state of pure unity;
this may be described as having great aspirations while possessing limited capacity.
Previously...
I earnestly entreated Master Yuanwu.
The Master bestowed upon me six sections of dharma discourse.
The first directly pointed to this very matter.
Later, he cited the two kōans concerning Yunmen’s “Put it down” and Zhaozhou’s “The Mount Sumeru”—
intending to have those of dull faculties constantly maintain self-awareness.
After a long time, there will surely be a point of entry;
such is the urgency of this compassionate heart.
Yet, alas, the dullness and stagnation are too extreme.
Now, fortunately, my worldly entanglements in private life have come to an end;
dwelling in leisure with no other affairs,
I shall simply exert myself with rigorous self-urging to fulfill my original aspiration.
My only regret is that I have not yet been able to receive your personal instruction.
I have presented each and every one of my life’s failures and shortcomings;
you will surely be able to clearly perceive this mind.
I hope you will provide detailed instructions on how one should practice in daily life,
so that I may avoid straying into other paths.
To directly equate this with the local [Chinese] context is to leave many flaws unaddressed.
Such a way of speaking leaves much to be desired.
However, as I am now casting myself in sincere devotion, it is difficult for me to remain hidden or escape;
since I am truly worthy of compassion,
I have come to knock at your door.
As you have related,
since my youth until my entry into official service, I have paid homage to many great masters; however, during that interval,
I was occupied by the demands of the civil service examinations, marriage, and official duties.
Furthermore, being overcome by evil thoughts and evil habits,
one is unable to practice with single-minded devotion;
this constitutes a grave transgression.
Furthermore, you are able to deeply contemplate impermanence and how the various phenomena of this world are illusory,
with not a single thing to be enjoyed; that you focus your mind on investigating this great matter of cause and condition is most agreeable to this sick monk’s heart.
However, since one has become a scholar who relies on a salary for a livelihood,
such matters as the civil service examinations, marriage,
and official appointment are things that cannot be avoided in this world.
Nor is it the fault of the noble one.
That he gives rise to great fear over a minor offense is not because he has,
throughout the vast kalpas of beginningless time, served true spiritual friends and cultivated the seeds of prajñā-wisdom.
How could one possibly avoid being like this?
Furthermore, as for what you call "great sins," even sages and worthies cannot escape them.
Knowing only that [all things] are illusory and not ultimate dharmas,
one is able to turn the mind toward this gateway and,
with the water of Prajñā-wisdom, [wash away delusions].
Having washed away the filth of defilements and dwelling in purity,
[he] cuts from below the feet, dividing it into two pieces.
It is sufficient that the mind of continuity does not arise again;
there is no need to contemplate what preceded or followed.
Since it is said to be empty and illusory.
Thus, the time of its arising is also an illusion;
the time of its experiencing is also an illusion;
and the time of its being cognized is also an illusion.
The time of delusion is also an illusion;
the past, present, and future are all entirely illusions.
Today one realizes they are not real.
Thus, one treats illusory ailments with illusory medicines;
once the illness has been cured, the medicine is discarded.
In the end, it remains simply the person of former times.
If there were a separate person or a separate dharma,
that would be the view of a demonic outsider;
you must reflect upon this deeply.
Simply proceed as if walking along this precipice.

From time to time, amidst moments of profound stillness and excellence, you must by no means forget these two phrases: "Mount Sumeru" and "Let it go. Simply proceed from beneath your feet with genuine earnestness.
One need not fear one's own transgressions,
nor is it necessary to dwell upon them;
for such dwelling in fear obstructs the Path.
However, before all the Buddhas,
one should make a great vow,
wishing that this mind be firm and steadfast.
Never falling back,
relying upon the empowerment of all Buddhas,
one encounters a good spiritual friend through a single word.
Suddenly casting off birth and death,
they realize and witness unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
thereby continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
This is to repay the incomparable kindness of all Buddhas.
If one proceeds in this manner, there is no reason why, after a long time, one would not attain enlightenment.
Have you not seen how the youth Sudhana set his mind on awakening under Mañjuśrī?
Traveling southward by stages, he passed through one hundred and ten cities and met fifty-three spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). Finally,
in the time it takes Maitreya to snap his fingers— *ekacchatāṅguliprasāraṇakāla*— he attained realization.
Suddenly, he forgot all the dharma-gates he had previously attained from his various spiritual mentors.
Following the instructions of Maitreya, he desired to pay homage to Mañjuśrī;
thereupon, Mañjuśrī reached out his right hand from afar.
Having traveled one hundred and ten yojanas,
he placed his hand upon Sudhana’s head and said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Good son, if one is devoid of the faculty of faith,
the mind will become inferior, depressed, and full of regret.
Their meritorious practices being incomplete,
they fall away from their diligent efforts and develop a mind of attachment toward a single root of goodness.
They consider even a small amount of merit to be sufficient;
they are unable to skillfully initiate practices and vows,
and they are not sustained or protected by spiritual friends.
They were unable to comprehend such a nature of phenomena,
such a principle, or such a gateway to the Dharma.
If one thoroughly understands such conduct and such objects of experience.
Whether it be various kinds of knowledge,
whether it be reaching the very source and bottom,
or whether it be thorough understanding.
Whether entering into it,
explaining it, or analyzing it.
Neither can they realize it, nor can they attain it.
Mañjuśrī thus proclaimed this to Sudhana.
At those words, Sudhana attained incalculable dharma-gates and became fully endowed with the immeasurable light of great wisdom.
Entering the gateway of Samantabhadra,
within a single thought-moment, they see as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm,
and they draw near to them all.
Respectfully serving and practicing their teachings,
one attains the wisdom of non-forgetfulness.
The liberation of the Treasury of Adornments,
by which one enters the lands within the pores of Samantabhadra;
taking a single step within a single pore.
Passing through worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
[he was] equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas.
Their buddha-fields, their practices,
and their mastery over liberation are all entirely equal,
without duality or distinction.
At such a time, one is finally able to transform the three poisons into the three groups of pure precepts,
and transform the six consciousnesses into the six supernormal powers.
Transforming afflictions into bodhi;
transforming ignorance into great wisdom.
Such is the sequence described above.
It depends solely upon the single, final moment of true realization of the person.
Even within the time it takes Maitreya to snap his fingers,
Sudhana was able to suddenly lose all the samādhis realized by his spiritual mentors.
How much more so for the habitual tendencies of false and evil karma from beginningless time?
If one takes the grave sins committed in the past as real, then all present and immediate objects of experience must likewise be considered truly existent.
Even official rank, wealth, nobility, and the bonds of affection—
all these are real. Since they are real,
[they are subject to suffering].
Thus, hell and heaven are real;
afflictions and ignorance are real;
and the agent of karma is also real.
The one who receives the retribution is also real;
the dharma-gate of the realized ground is also real.
If you hold such a view, [you have not yet understood].
Then, until the end of the future,
there would be no one at all who could enter the Buddha-vehicle.
[This would contradict] the Buddhas of the three periods and the successive patriarchs of all generations.
Various skillful means are,
conversely, rendered as false speech.
This was when you, Master Cheng, sent the letter.
He burned incense before the various saints and paid remote prostrations to the hermitage before dispatching [the messenger].
His sincerity was thus most profound.
Although we are not very far apart,
we have not yet had the opportunity for face-to-face conversation; thus, I write this letter with my sincere heart and by the hand of faith.
I was unaware that it had become so extensive;
though it may seem prolix,
it nonetheless issues from a heart of utmost sincerity.
I dare not deceive you with a single word or a single character.
To deceive you would be nothing less than to deceive myself.
Furthermore, I recall:
Sudhana beheld the brahmin Most Tranquil and attained the liberation of truthful speech regarding all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future.
Regarding unexcelled bodhi,
they have never regressed in the past, do not regress in the present,
and shall not regress in the future; whatever they seek is invariably fulfilled.
All this is reached through the power of ultimate sincerity.
Since you have taken a bamboo chair and a rush mat as your companions,
you are no different from Sudhana meeting the most serene Brahmin.
Furthermore, he sent a letter to Yunmen,
dispatching it after first performing prostrations from afar to all the saints;
his sole purpose was to seek Yunmen’s trust and approval.
This is indeed a most urgent matter.
Simply listen to me:
practice your cultivation exactly as I have described.
In the future, you will undoubtedly attain the fulfillment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore,
Your Excellency dwells in wealth and nobility.
Yet they are not broken or distressed by wealth and status.
Were it not for having planted the seeds of prajñā-wisdom in former lives, how could they be thus?
I only fear that you might forget this meaning midway,
being hindered by your sharp faculties and intelligence,
and placing the mind of "attainment" before you all at once.
Therefore, one cannot directly cut through the ancient masters' most direct and essential points with a single stroke to find immediate rest.
This ailment affects not only scholars and gentlemen,
but long-term practitioners as well.
Most are unwilling to retreat and apply their efforts where it is easy;
they merely employ their clever conscious intellect for calculation and deliberation,
racing outward in pursuit of external things.
When first hearing that a teacher of knowledge uses the intellect and consciousness for deliberation and calculation, while outwardly presenting the fodder of one's own fundamental nature,
people mostly miss the mark right before their faces.
They assume this is merely the way of the ancient worthies of old.
There are actual dharmas given to people,
such as Zhaozhou’s “Let it drop” and Yunmen’s “Mount Sumeru,” and so forth. Yantou said:
To withdraw from things is superior;
to pursue things is inferior.
It is also said:
To grasp the great governing principles and the fundamental tenets,
one must necessarily recognize the "phrase. What is this phrase?
The time when there is no thought of a hundred things is called the "correct phrase" (zhengju).
It is also called "dwelling on the summit" and "attaining stability."
